items.def: how much work a person, team or machine produces in a particular amount of time
items.ex: Many managers believe that shorter meetings lead to higher productivity, as employees have more uninterrupted time to focus.

items.def: to make a process or machine work by itself, without a person controlling each step
items.ex: As banks automate routine tasks such as checking documents, fewer staff are needed in local branches.

items.def: a general rise in prices over time, which means that the same amount of money buys less than before
items.ex: When inflation rises faster than wages, ordinary families find it harder to pay for basic goods such as food and fuel.

items.def: all the people who work for a company or in an industry or country
items.ex: An ageing workforce means that many countries will soon face a shortage of experienced nurses and engineers.

items.def: no longer used or needed because something newer and better has taken its place
items.ex: Some people fear that many of today's jobs will become obsolete within a generation because of automation.

items.def: something, such as money or a reward, that encourages a person to do something or to work harder
items.ex: Financial incentives such as bonuses can motivate staff, but they may also encourage unhealthy competition between colleagues.
col: a strong incentive to do sth

items.def: the money that a government receives from taxes, or that a business earns from selling its goods or services
items.ex: Governments could use the revenue from a tax on sugary drinks to fund public health campaigns.

items.def: an important new discovery or development, often one that comes after a long period of effort
items.ex: Recent breakthroughs in battery technology have made electric cars far more practical for long journeys.

items.def: a state of complete physical and mental tiredness and lost motivation, caused by working too hard for too long
items.ex: Long working hours and constant pressure to answer emails at night are major causes of burnout among young professionals.

items.def: to pay part of the cost of something so that it becomes cheaper for the people who use it
items.ex: If the government subsidised public transport, more commuters might be willing to leave their cars at home.

items.def: the newest and most advanced of its kind
items.ex: Hospitals that invest in cutting-edge equipment can diagnose some diseases much earlier than before.
col: at the cutting edge of sth
items.ar: متطور، أحدث ما توصّل إليه العلم

items.def: an arrangement that lets employees choose when or where they work, for example from home or with different hours
items.ex: Flexible working allows parents to collect their children from school without sacrificing their careers.

items.def: how cheap or expensive something is compared with the amount of money people have
items.ex: The affordability of housing has become a serious concern for young people in many large cities.

items.def: the basic systems and structures that a country or organisation needs in order to work, such as roads, power supplies and communication networks
items.ex: Rural areas will not benefit from online services unless governments invest in broadband infrastructure.

items.def: to give part of your work or responsibility to another person, usually someone below you in an organisation
items.ex: Effective managers delegate routine tasks so that they can concentrate on long-term planning.

items.def: money put into a business, project or service in order to make a profit or gain a benefit in the future; also time or effort used in this way
items.ex: Investment in public transport pays off in the long term by reducing traffic congestion and pollution.

items.def: a new idea, method or product, or the process of creating new ones
items.ex: Governments can encourage innovation by funding research and offering tax relief to small technology firms.

items.def: to work together with other people or organisations in order to achieve something
items.ex: Online tools make it easy for engineers in different countries to collaborate on the same project in real time.

items.def: the state of being successful and having enough money, especially for a whole country or community
items.ex: Some economists argue that long-term prosperity depends more on a well-educated population than on natural resources.

items.def: the ability of computer systems to do tasks that normally need human thinking, such as understanding language or recognising images
items.ex: Artificial intelligence can help doctors detect illnesses earlier, but the final decision about treatment should remain with a human.

items.def: doing your job from home or from another place away from the main office, using the internet to stay in contact
items.ex: Remote working has saved millions of people hours of travelling, yet some employees miss the social side of office life.

items.def: a period when a country's economy becomes smaller, businesses sell less and unemployment usually rises
items.ex: During a recession, young graduates often struggle to find their first job and may accept work below their skill level.

items.def: the skills needed to use digital devices and the internet effectively, safely and with good judgement
items.ex: Schools should teach digital literacy from an early age so that children can tell reliable websites from misleading ones.

items.def: a healthy division of your time and energy between your job and your family, rest and personal interests
items.ex: A healthy work-life balance is now as important to many job seekers as a high salary.

items.def: an increase over time in the amount of goods and services that a country produces
items.ex: Rapid economic growth can lift millions out of poverty, but it often comes at a cost to the environment.

items.def: the gap between people who have easy access to computers and the internet and people who do not
items.ex: The sudden move to online learning during school closures widened the digital divide between rich and poor families.

items.def: the feeling of pleasure and achievement that a person gets from doing their job
items.ex: For many employees, job satisfaction depends more on feeling valued than on pay alone.

items.def: the situation in which people who want to work cannot find a job; also the number of people in this situation
items.ex: High youth unemployment can lead to frustration and social unrest if it continues for many years.

items.def: easy to learn and simple to use, even for people with little technical knowledge
items.ex: Government websites must be user-friendly so that elderly citizens can access services without asking for help.

items.def: the amount of work that a person or organisation has to do
items.ex: Teachers often complain that their workload has grown because of paperwork rather than actual teaching.

items.def: the amount of money that a person needs to pay for basic things such as food, housing and transport
items.ex: The rising cost of living has forced many young adults to stay in their parents' home for longer than they would like.

items.def: to improve a machine, system or service, or to replace it with a newer and better version
items.ex: Many consumers feel pressured to upgrade their phones every year, even when the old one still works perfectly.

items.def: to travel regularly between your home and your place of work or study
items.ex: Employees who commute for two hours a day have far less time for exercise and family life.

items.def: a person or company that pays tax to the government
items.ex: Critics argue that taxpayers' money should not be spent on luxury stadiums that only a minority of citizens will use.

items.def: to change something completely, usually in a way that improves it
items.ex: Smartphones have revolutionised the way people shop, bank and keep in touch with relatives abroad.
col: revolutionise the way sth is done

items.def: working for several different clients on separate projects, rather than being employed full-time by one company
items.ex: Freelance designers enjoy choosing their own projects, but they have no guaranteed income at the end of each month.

items.def: the lowest amount of pay per hour that employers are legally allowed to pay their workers
items.ex: Raising the minimum wage could reduce poverty, although some small businesses claim it would force them to cut jobs.

items.def: the ability of devices, people or places to connect to the internet or to each other
items.ex: Better connectivity in rural villages would allow local businesses to sell their products online.

items.def: working for yourself and running your own business, instead of being employed by a company
items.ex: Being self-employed offers freedom, but it also means paying for your own pension and taking unpaid holidays.

items.def: knowing a lot about modern technology and feeling confident when using it
items.ex: Although young people are often described as tech-savvy, many of them struggle to judge whether online information is reliable.

items.def: the total amount of money that ordinary people spend on goods and services
items.ex: When consumer spending falls, shops and restaurants are often the first businesses to close.

items.def: a person who starts their own business, often taking financial risks in the hope of making a profit
items.ex: Young entrepreneurs can now reach customers all over the world through social media without renting a shop.

items.def: a new technology that is still being developed but is expected to have a large effect in the future
items.ex: Emerging technologies such as gene editing raise ethical questions that the law has not yet answered.

items.def: to find new people and persuade them to join a company or organisation
items.ex: Rural hospitals find it difficult to recruit doctors unless they offer higher salaries or free accommodation.

items.def: a small new company, often one built around a new product or technology
items.ex: Many tech start-ups fail within a few years because they run out of money before they make a profit.

items.def: an attempt by criminals or governments to damage, disrupt or steal information from computer systems
items.ex: A single cyberattack on a hospital's computer system could put patients' lives at risk.

items.def: time that a person works in addition to their normal working hours, or the extra money paid for this
items.ex: Some factory workers depend on overtime to support their families because their basic pay is so low.

items.def: a large company that has offices or factories in several different countries
items.ex: When a multinational opens a factory in a developing country, it creates jobs but may also force small local firms out of business.

items.def: the right of people to control how information about them is collected, stored and shared
items.ex: If data privacy is to be respected, users must be told clearly how an app will use their personal details.

items.def: the confidence that you will be able to keep your job for a long time
items.ex: In the past, many workers valued job security above everything else and stayed with one employer for life.

items.def: the level of comfort, money and goods that a person or community has
items.ex: Cheap imported goods have arguably raised the standard of living of ordinary families, even if some local factories have closed.

items.def: a website or app that allows people or businesses to communicate, share content or buy and sell things
items.ex: Online platforms that connect drivers with passengers have transformed the taxi industry in many cities.

items.def: moving to more senior and better-paid positions during your working life
items.ex: Employees are more likely to stay with a company if they can see clear opportunities for career progression.

items.def: the buying and selling of goods and services on the internet
items.ex: The growth of e-commerce has contributed to the closure of many high-street shops in small towns.

items.def: the ability of a group of people to work well together to reach a shared goal
items.ex: Group projects at university help students develop teamwork, which employers consider an essential skill.

items.def: a cost or debt that is difficult for a person, family or government to pay
items.ex: Caring for elderly relatives can place a heavy financial burden on working families.
col: place a financial burden on sb

items.def: a small device or tool that does a particular job, often in a clever or new way
items.ex: Many households are full of electronic gadgets that are rarely used after the first few weeks.

items.def: the period of your life after you stop working, usually because of your age
items.ex: As people live longer, many governments are raising the retirement age to keep pension systems affordable.

items.def: allowing two-way communication between a user and a computer or program, so that the user's actions change what happens
items.ex: Interactive quizzes and simulations can keep young learners more engaged than traditional textbooks.

items.def: a society in which people pay for almost everything by card or phone rather than with notes and coins
items.ex: A cashless society may be convenient for most people, but it could exclude elderly citizens who do not use digital banking.
col: the rise of a cashless society
items.ar: مجتمع غير نقدي، مجتمع بلا نقود ورقية

items.def: physical work done with the hands or body rather than with the mind or with machines
items.ex: As robots take over heavy manual labour, factory workers will need training for more technical roles.

items.def: created by a computer or existing online, rather than in the physical world
items.ex: Virtual tours allow students to explore famous museums without the cost of travelling abroad.

items.def: a short period of work, often done by students or recent graduates, to gain experience in a particular job
items.ex: Unpaid internships are unfair because only young people with wealthy parents can afford to accept them.

items.def: the science and technology of designing, building and using robots
items.ex: Advances in robotics mean that dangerous jobs, such as inspecting underwater pipelines, can be done without risking human lives.

items.def: practical experience gained by doing a job yourself, rather than only reading or hearing about it
items.ex: Apprenticeships give school leavers hands-on experience that a classroom alone cannot provide.

items.def: able to travel without a human driver because a computer controls it
items.ex: Driverless cars could reduce accidents caused by tiredness, but they raise difficult questions about legal responsibility.

items.def: a belief in the value of hard work, together with the habit of working hard and responsibly
items.ex: Part-time jobs can help teenagers develop a strong work ethic and learn how to manage money.

items.def: a person who secretly gets into other people's computer systems, often to steal information or cause damage
items.ex: Hackers increasingly target small businesses, which often have weaker security than large corporations.

items.def: a working arrangement in which employees work four days instead of five, usually for the same pay
items.ex: Supporters of a four-day week claim that staff can remain just as productive while feeling far less stressed.

items.def: false or inaccurate information, especially when it spreads widely, whether or not people intend to mislead
items.ex: Social media companies should do more to stop misinformation from spreading during health emergencies.

items.def: doing several tasks at the same time, or switching quickly from one task to another
items.ex: Although multitasking feels efficient, constantly switching between emails and reports can lower the quality of work.

items.def: watching or listening to films, music or videos over the internet while they are being sent, without downloading them first
items.ex: The popularity of streaming has changed television, since viewers now decide for themselves what to watch and when.

items.def: the screens, buttons and menus through which a person controls a computer program, website or app
items.ex: A clear user interface can make a banking app usable even for people with poor eyesight or limited computer skills.

items.def: crimes in which people are tricked into giving away money or personal details over the internet
items.ex: Older people are often the main victims of online fraud because criminals pretend to be calling from their bank.

items.def: designed to reduce the amount of physical work that people need to do
items.ex: Labour-saving devices such as washing machines gave many women more time to enter paid employment in the twentieth century.

items.def: progress in the development of technology, which produces new and better machines, tools or methods
items.ex: Rapid technological advancement means that some skills learnt at university may be out of date within a decade.

items.def: a set of step-by-step rules that a computer follows to solve a problem or make a decision
items.ex: Social media algorithms tend to show users content they already agree with, which can make their opinions more extreme.

items.def: the situation in which an employer ends someone's job because the job is no longer needed
items.ex: When the factory introduced robots, hundreds of workers faced redundancy with very little support to retrain.
items.ar: التسريح من العمل، الاستغناء عن الموظف

items.def: the money a person has left to spend or save after paying tax and essential bills
items.ex: When housing costs rise, young families have less disposable income for leisure activities and saving.

items.def: the careful watching of people or places, often by the police, a government or a company, using cameras or digital data
items.ex: While surveillance cameras may deter crime, constant monitoring could make citizens feel that their privacy is being ignored.

items.def: (formal) the money and other benefits that a person receives for the work they do
items.ex: Remuneration in the public sector often fails to reflect the level of responsibility carried by nurses and teachers.

items.def: causing a big change in the way an industry or activity works, often by replacing older products or businesses
items.ex: Disruptive technologies such as online banking have forced traditional banks to close many of their branches.

items.def: the amount of goods and services that a sum of money, or a group of people, is able to buy
items.ex: Inflation steadily reduces the purchasing power of pensioners whose income stays the same.

items.def: the process of changing information into a secret code so that only people with permission can read it
items.ex: Strong encryption protects people's messages from criminals, although some governments argue that it also helps criminals hide their plans.

items.def: a meeting in which a manager judges how well an employee has worked and discusses goals for the future
items.ex: Regular appraisals give employees a chance to discuss their progress and request further training.

items.def: a type of artificial intelligence in which computers get better at a task by finding patterns in large amounts of data
items.ex: Machine learning allows online shops to predict what customers want before they even search for it.
col: use machine learning to do sth

items.def: a labour market in which many people do short-term tasks or contracts, often found through apps, instead of having permanent jobs
items.ex: The gig economy gives workers flexibility, but it often leaves them without sick pay or a pension.
col: the rise of the gig economy
items.ar: اقتصاد العمل الحر المؤقت، اقتصاد المهام

items.def: producing a large amount of money or profit
items.ex: Some talented graduates choose lucrative careers in finance rather than becoming teachers or researchers.

items.def: an incident in which private information is stolen or seen by people who should not have access to it
items.ex: After a major data breach, customers may lose trust in a company even if no money was taken.

items.def: an extra benefit that you get from your job in addition to your salary, such as free meals or a company car
items.ex: Free gym membership and flexible hours are perks that help technology firms attract young talent.

items.def: the use of computer services, such as storage and software, that are provided over the internet instead of on your own device
items.ex: Cloud computing allows small companies to use powerful software without buying expensive equipment.

items.def: a system in which people are arranged in levels according to their power or importance
items.ex: In companies with a rigid hierarchy, junior staff may hesitate to share new ideas with senior managers.

items.def: a tax that a government charges on goods coming into or leaving a country
items.ex: Raising tariffs on imported cars may protect local manufacturers, but consumers usually end up paying more.

items.def: the record of everything a person does online, such as the websites they visit and the things they post
items.ex: Teenagers should understand that their digital footprint may be seen by universities and employers in the future.

items.def: the rate at which employees leave an organisation and have to be replaced
items.ex: High staff turnover is expensive because each new employee needs time and training before becoming fully productive.

items.def: the network of everyday objects, such as fridges, watches and heating systems, that are connected to the internet and can share data
items.ex: The Internet of Things could make homes more energy-efficient, for example by switching off the heating when nobody is in.
col: connected to the Internet of Things

items.def: to sell a company or service that is owned by the government to private owners
items.ex: Supporters claim that privatising the railways would improve efficiency, while opponents fear higher fares.

items.def: the habit of regularly staying away from work or school without a good reason
items.ex: Companies that look after their employees' mental health often see a fall in absenteeism.

items.def: using the most modern ideas, methods or equipment that are available
items.ex: The new library offers state-of-the-art facilities, including quiet study rooms and free high-speed internet.

items.def: the level of confidence, enthusiasm and satisfaction that a person or group feels at a particular time
items.ex: Repeated job cuts can damage staff morale, even among employees who manage to keep their jobs.

items.def: complete control of a market by one company, so that there is no real competition
items.ex: When one company has a monopoly on internet services, it can raise prices without fear of losing customers.

items.def: the arrival or beginning of an important new invention, idea or period
items.ex: Since the advent of the smartphone, people rarely need to memorise phone numbers or directions.

items.def: to pay another company, often in another country, to do work that used to be done inside your own organisation
items.ex: Many firms outsource their customer service to countries where wages are lower.

items.def: the percentage that a bank charges for lending money, or pays you for keeping your savings
items.ex: Low interest rates encourage people to borrow and spend, but they offer little reward to savers.

items.def: depending on something too much, so that you cannot manage without it
items.ex: An over-reliance on calculators may prevent children from developing basic mental arithmetic skills.

items.def: to learn new skills, or to teach workers new skills, especially so that they can do a more modern job
items.ex: Rather than replacing older staff, companies should upskill them to work alongside new digital systems.

items.def: easy to understand and use without needing instructions
items.ex: An intuitive app design means that even first-time users can complete a task without reading a manual.

items.def: a situation in which there are not enough workers available to fill the jobs that exist
items.ex: Some countries are tackling labour shortages in healthcare by recruiting nurses from abroad.

items.def: abilities, such as communication or problem-solving, that are useful in many different jobs
items.ex: Volunteering helps young people build transferable skills that will be valuable in almost any career.

items.def: happening smoothly, without problems, pauses or obvious changes from one part to the next
items.ex: Customers now expect a seamless experience when they move from a shop's website to its mobile app.

items.def: the illegal act of not paying the tax that you owe
items.ex: When wealthy individuals engage in tax evasion, ordinary citizens end up carrying a greater share of the tax burden.

items.def: able to operate or make decisions independently, without human control
items.ex: Autonomous delivery robots could one day bring groceries to people's doors without a human courier.

items.def: to control every small detail of other people's work instead of trusting them to do it themselves
items.ex: Managers who micromanage their teams often reduce motivation and slow down decision-making.
items.ar: يُفرط في التدخل في أدق التفاصيل

items.def: a weakness in a computer system or program that attackers could use to get in or cause harm
items.ex: Software companies release regular updates to fix vulnerabilities before criminals can exploit them.

items.def: a period in which business activity and the economy become weaker
items.ex: During an economic downturn, luxury goods are usually among the first purchases that families cut back on.
col: a downturn in the housing market

items.def: an unofficial barrier that stops women or members of minority groups from reaching the most senior jobs
items.ex: Despite having equal qualifications, many women still hit a glass ceiling when they apply for board-level positions.

items.def: the situation in which other people do not know who you are
items.ex: Online anonymity allows people to speak freely, but it also makes it easier to post abusive comments without consequences.

items.def: to encourage something, such as spending or business activity, to grow or become more active
items.ex: Cutting taxes for small businesses could stimulate the local economy and create jobs.

items.def: to stop employing workers, sometimes temporarily, because there is not enough work or money
items.ex: When demand for flights fell sharply, the airline laid off a third of its cabin crew.

items.def: a small fault in a machine or computer program that stops it from working properly
items.ex: A minor technical glitch in the booking system left thousands of passengers unable to check in online.

items.def: a system in which different groups of employees work at different times of the day or night, so that a workplace can operate around the clock
items.ex: Years of shift work can disrupt sleep patterns and increase the risk of long-term health problems.

items.def: for each person in a population; used to compare figures between countries or regions of different sizes
items.ex: Although the country's total wealth is enormous, income per capita remains below the regional average.

items.def: relating to people who work in offices and do mental rather than physical work
items.ex: Artificial intelligence may threaten white-collar jobs, such as accounting and legal research, more than manual ones.

items.def: describes software whose original code is freely available for anyone to use, study and change
items.ex: Open-source software lets developers around the world improve a program together instead of paying for a licence.

items.def: a digital form of money that is not controlled by a central bank and uses secure codes to record transactions
items.ex: The value of a cryptocurrency can rise or fall dramatically in a single day, which makes it a risky investment.

items.def: the difference between the skills that employers need and the skills that available workers actually have
items.ex: Closer cooperation between universities and businesses could help close the skills gap in engineering.

items.def: a very large and powerful technology company
items.ex: Some politicians argue that tech giants have become so powerful that they should be broken up into smaller companies.

items.def: raising money for a project by asking a large number of people to give small amounts, usually online
items.ex: Crowdfunding has allowed independent inventors to launch new products without relying on bank loans.

items.def: the movement of highly skilled and educated people from one country to another where pay and conditions are better
items.ex: The brain drain of doctors to wealthier nations leaves hospitals in their home countries seriously understaffed.
col: a brain drain of skilled workers

items.def: to change documents, pictures or services into a digital form that computers can store and use
items.ex: Digitising medical records allows doctors in different hospitals to see a patient's full history instantly.

items.def: an organisation of workers that aims to protect their rights and improve their pay and working conditions
items.ex: Trade unions argue that gig workers deserve the same basic protections as permanent employees.

items.def: to find the cause of a problem in a system, machine or piece of software and fix it
items.ex: As a developer, I spend a surprising amount of time troubleshooting small layout problems that appear only on certain browsers.

items.def: the crime of using another person's personal details, such as their name or bank information, to steal money or obtain services
items.ex: Sharing too much personal information on social media can make people easy targets for identity theft.

items.def: based on collecting and carefully studying data rather than on guesses or personal opinions
items.ex: Data-driven planning allows city councils to put new bus routes exactly where they are most needed.

items.def: a situation in which you receive so much information that you cannot think clearly or make decisions
items.ex: Constant notifications create information overload, making it harder for students to concentrate on a single task.

items.def: electronic devices, such as smartwatches and fitness trackers, that people wear on their bodies
items.ex: Wearable technology can encourage people to exercise more by tracking their steps and heart rate throughout the day.

items.def: found or seen almost everywhere
items.ex: Smartphones have become so ubiquitous that it is hard to imagine a train journey without passengers staring at screens.
items.ar: واسع الانتشار، موجود في كل مكان

items.def: a government policy of sharply cutting public spending in order to reduce debt
items.ex: Years of austerity left many public libraries and youth centres without enough money to stay open.

items.def: not safe or certain and likely to get worse; often used about jobs without security or a regular income
items.ex: Many young graduates are stuck in precarious jobs with short contracts and no guarantee of regular hours.

items.def: a sudden and rapid increase in the number or amount of something
items.ex: The proliferation of food delivery apps has changed the way many city residents eat.

items.def: entering someone's private life in a way that is unwelcome or annoying
items.ex: Many users find targeted advertising intrusive, especially when it seems to know about conversations they had offline.

items.def: relating to government money, especially taxes and public spending
items.ex: Fiscal measures, such as higher taxes on luxury goods, could be used to fund better public services.

items.def: an online space in which people mainly hear opinions that match their own, so their views are rarely challenged
items.ex: Social media can become an echo chamber in which users only follow people who share their political beliefs.

items.def: the unfair practice of giving jobs or advantages to relatives or friends, especially by people in power
items.ex: Transparent recruitment procedures are essential to prevent nepotism in public institutions.

items.def: the practice of designing products so that they break or go out of date quickly, forcing people to buy new ones
items.ex: Planned obsolescence not only costs consumers money but also adds to the growing problem of electronic waste.

items.def: a situation in which an economy, wages or a business stop growing or developing
items.ex: A long period of wage stagnation can leave workers feeling that hard work is no longer rewarded.

items.def: a job agreement in which the employer does not have to offer the worker any minimum number of hours
items.ex: Workers on zero-hours contracts find it almost impossible to plan their finances or obtain a mortgage.

items.def: describing an imagined future society in which life is extremely unpleasant, often because of technology or an unjust government
items.ex: Critics of facial recognition warn that constant monitoring could lead to a dystopian future with no privacy at all.

items.def: the policy of protecting a country's own industries by taxing or limiting imports
items.ex: Although protectionism may save some local jobs in the short term, it often leads to higher prices and weaker trade relations.

items.def: the habit of going to work when you are ill, or staying longer than necessary to look committed, often while achieving very little
items.ex: Presenteeism may look like dedication, but staff who come to work while ill often spread infections and achieve little.

items.def: to skip a stage of development and move straight to a more advanced level
items.ex: Some developing countries have leapfrogged landline telephones and moved directly to mobile networks.
items.ar: يتجاوز المراحل، يقفز إلى مرحلة متقدمة

items.def: the knowledge, skills and health of a country's people or a company's staff, seen as a source of economic value
items.ex: Investing in education and healthcare builds human capital, which is the foundation of long-term economic success.

items.def: a long period of paid or unpaid time away from work, often used to study, travel or rest
items.ex: Allowing experienced staff to take a sabbatical can reduce burnout and bring fresh ideas back to the company.

items.def: unfair results produced by a computer system, often because it learnt from data that reflected existing human prejudices
items.ex: If recruitment software is trained on past hiring decisions, algorithmic bias may lead it to reject well-qualified female applicants.

items.def: treating workers or other people unfairly in order to profit from their work
items.ex: Consumers can discourage exploitative labour practices by refusing to buy clothes from brands that underpay factory workers.

items.def: the removal of government rules and controls from an industry or market
items.ex: Deregulating an industry can lower prices for consumers, but it may also weaken protections for workers.

items.def: able to grow or serve many more people without losing quality or becoming much more expensive
items.ex: Online courses are highly scalable, since one recorded lecture can reach thousands of learners at almost no extra cost.

items.def: action, such as a strike, that workers take to protest about their pay or working conditions
items.ex: Nurses rarely take industrial action, so when they do, it usually reflects deep frustration with their working conditions.

items.def: using measurements of a person's body, such as fingerprints or facial features, to identify them
items.ex: Biometric passports have made border checks faster, but they also mean that sensitive personal data is held by governments.

items.def: moving money from richer people to poorer people, usually through taxes and public services
items.ex: Supporters of higher inheritance taxes see them as a fair way to achieve some redistribution of wealth.
col: call for the redistribution of wealth

items.def: a risk or danger that is a normal part of a particular job
items.ex: Back pain is an occupational hazard for anyone who spends eight hours a day sitting at a computer.

items.def: to find a clever way of avoiding a rule, restriction or system
items.ex: Teenagers often find ways to circumvent parental controls, so teaching responsible use is more effective than simply blocking websites.

items.def: sudden and frequent changes in prices on a market, which make investing risky
items.ex: Market volatility can discourage ordinary families from investing their savings in shares.

items.def: small problems that happen in the early stages of a new system, product or project
items.ex: The new online ticketing system had a few teething problems, but most passengers now find it faster than queuing.

items.def: to find a skilled person who already works for another company and persuade them to join yours
items.ex: Talented software engineers are often headhunted by larger firms that can offer higher salaries.

items.def: to change or interfere with something without permission, usually in order to damage it or to cheat
items.ex: Electronic voting systems must be designed so that no one can tamper with the results.

items.def: the process of replacing permanent, secure jobs with temporary or irregular work
items.ex: The casualisation of university teaching means that many lecturers now move from one short contract to the next.
items.ar: تحويل الوظائف الدائمة إلى عمل مؤقت

items.def: a person who dislikes new technology or refuses to use it
items.ex: Refusing to use online banking does not make my grandfather a Luddite; he simply trusts face-to-face service more.

items.def: money that an employer pays to a worker whose job has been ended
items.ex: Generous severance pay can help redundant workers support their families while they retrain for a new career.

items.def: discussions between a trade union and an employer to agree pay and working conditions for a whole group of workers
items.ex: Collective bargaining gives individual workers a stronger voice than they would have if they negotiated alone.
